#6660. Buying Your First Pair of Selvedge Jeans? Start Here

We’ve got bad news for white couches: Crunchy, indigo-dyed, raw selvedge jeans are back. People might say they never left, but as someone who literally edited a daily web series about denim fades from 2015 to 2018, I can assure you that across the almost-decade since, the category has taken something of a back seat as jeans with interesting washes and nostalgic cuts (Our Legacy’s Third Cut, GAP’s 90s Loose) surged in popularity.

But while it, ahem, faded from the public eye, the raw denim market was still tended to by the true believers among us. And we owe them a great debt, because their stewardship means we’re not just picking up where the last trend left off. Instead, we’re jumping into an elevated timeline. The best makers in the world have only gotten better, the cuts have gotten more diverse, and a whole bunch of stuff that was once incredibly hard to find in the United States is now readily available.

So available, in fact, that the selection can be overwhelming. Which is where I come in! Because while there are now thousands of pairs of raw denim jeans to choose from, I can tell you that only a precious few specific cuts have consistently dominated Subreddits, YouTube roundups, and my text message history for the best part of this century. Ten of them are below, starting with five approachable icons, and moving through to five more legendary deeper cuts. Let’s get faded.

The company behind Sugar Cane, Toyo Enterprise, has been making hard-wearing garments since the mid-’60s, but Sugar Cane didn’t come around until 1975. Ever since, they’ve been making some of the most considered, sturdy and timeless jeans and workwear on the planet in Japan, all of it aging more beautifully than a fancy barolo.

If you’re looking to dip your toes into the Sugar Cane pool, the 1947 model brilliantly recreates one of the most well-loved iterations of the most well-worn model on the planet (we won’t name names, but they’re in here too), and comes in a four-season, 14.25oz. selvedge denim fabric that will produce some preposterously good fades.

For anyone who’s fallen in love with a pair of old old vintage jeans, and wondered what they felt like when they came off the production line, it’s hard to get closer than a pair of Fullcounts. The brand was started in 1993 in Osaka, Japan, with the express purpose of reverse engineering the wonder of those vintage pairs, down to the all-cotton threads and long-staple cotton.

They sure figured it out, and still make everything in Japan. And while the classic 0105 is an absolute knockout, the Wide Straight iteration gives you a little more comfort with the same break-in potential. And if you’re just getting yourself into the raw selvedge game, a little comfort never hurts.

The only Canadian entrant on this list—partly because Henry’s hasn’t restocked yet—Naked & Famous has been around since 2008. And as you might expect from a brand whose hallmark fit is called the Weird Guy, they’re a little quirky. In a good way! For not only are they rigorously dedicated to sourcing the sickest raw denim on the planet, but that denim often has some funky detailing as well, like a green weft or some galaxy-like imperfections.

The True Guy cut is technically a relaxed straight (don’t confuse that for baggy) and this particular pair has kevlar woven into the fabric, for those into literal bulletproof denim.

If you’ve ever spent time on denim message boards, you’ve probably seen the name “Iron Heart” associated with some of the heaviest denim known to man. (If you’ve never been, steel yourself before entering.) And while it is true that the Japanese brand pushes the definition of heavyweight to its absolute limit, it also makes a damn good pair of regular jeans.

In fact, the mid-weight fare is as good as any on the market, will produce some HOF-worthy fades, and won’t require a title fight to soften up. Within that weight class, the straight leg of the 634S-142 is the kind of timeless silhouette that should outlast most trend cycles. (Also, for the record, “mid-weight” is a relative term. This is the lightest-weight denim that Iron Heart will entertain.)

While the US quite literally invented jeans as we understand them (denim as a fabric is another story, for those keeping very detailed score), you’d be forgiven for thinking otherwise, considering the lack of US-made options on this list. But thankfully, 3Sixteen is doing the work of like six companies at this point, sourcing the world’s finest denim—we don’t really make that here anymore—and stitching the 5-pockets up back home in the USA.

Every cut they make has a legion of fans, but the semi-recent, semi-baggy RS is the one tearing up the charts at the moment. And for great reasons. It’s got the aforementioned room, has a top block (re: the area that houses the waistband, fly and pockets) that doesn’t get all bunched up and funky, and a higher rise that’s flattering on just about everyone. As a result, it’s a pair that both denimheads and denim rookies appreciate with the same kind of zeal.

When it comes to details that will turn a denimhead into a living meme—Vince McMahon Progression, Guy Turning Around, you pick—few brands can execute them like Oni can. From the denim itself, which is milled in Japan and feels more handmade than small-batch sourdough, to the period-accurate details like flat-felled seams and linear bar tacks, every pair starts as a work of art and develops into a wholly separate work of art as they’re worn.

The only issue, really, is finding them, because hand-making just about everything isn’t exactly a scalable process. When they’re around, (and they currently are!) they’re worth more than just a gander, particularly the Wide Straight, which has a loose, straight leg and a healthy, fairly forgiving rise. This pair in particular is made with lighter-weight 12oz. denim, but don’t mistake that for lightweight denim—it’ll hold up year round, and could always handle some longjohns during a cold-snap, if you feel so inclined.

Those familiar with the Osaka 5—the loose collection of denim brands that sprouted up in Osaka in the ‘70s, ‘80s and ‘90s and redefined the very notion of raw denim specifically and the idea of what “jeans” could be, more broadly—will know that Warehouse was the fifth and final member, founded by two alums from a different member, Evisu. And for roughly 30 years the brand’s pumped out intricately detailed, vintage-indebted jeans that some of the pickiest people on the planet have sworn by, even going so far as sourcing American cotton to keep the look and feel as close to the source material as possible.

This pair in particular is based on one of the most popular pairs of 501s Levi’s ever made, the 1966 model, which had a straight leg and a high rise and a slightly twisted seam after a few washes, giving it a slow-developing signature—all present and accounted for here in 2026 via Warehouse.

These aren’t for the faint of heart. Let’s get that out of the way. 21oz. denim is almost armor, especially if your previous denim reference point is something with a wash, a rinse or some stretch. But for anyone looking for a challenge, absolutely electric fades and a pair of jeans that might outlast horseshoe crabs, look no further.

That’s because Samurai, another Osaka-based brand (but not part of the Osaka 5, for whatever it’s worth), makes some of the hardest-fading, hardest-wearing, most-revered jeans anywhere, and that includes the ultra-heavyweight numbers. And who knows, all that extra (fabric) weight might be nice with winter incoming.

Levi’s offers some great raw selvedge 501s at a pretty reasonable price, a pair that will age well and (with proper care of course) last for years. The 501, however, isn’t a standardized cut. In fact, it’s tweaked every few years to reflect the prevailing sentiment of the time a little bit better. And as a result, different eras have different hallmarks—for instance, the 1947 is a bit slimmer, the 1954 is the first pair with a zipper and the 1901 is the first pair with two back pockets.

Levi’s Vintage Clothing, a sub-label under the broader umbrella, still makes a bunch of these pairs and while the aforementioned are killer, the 1933 feels paradoxically relevant to 2026: it’s got a healthy, wide leg, a healthy rise and a couple cheeky details to differentiate it from the rest of the pack, like a back cinch and suspender buttons.

We couldn’t make this list without including a pair from the first member of the Osaka 5, in part because it’s hard to imagine any of this would be possible without Studio D’Artisan and in part because the brand still makes some of the best jeans in the world. Founded in 1979, Studio D’Artisan kicked off the obsession surrounding raw selvedge denim and bygone detailing, doubling down on craftsmanship and material quality in an era defined by synthetics and acid-washing. And they never really strayed, ultimately adding some more timeless staples to the denim assortment, all of it made in Japan with commensurate care. The SD-801 is a classic straight leg fit, made in Japan from a rope-dyed natural indigo 15oz. denim fabric and armed with a host of cheeky details, like a selvedge hit at the coin pocket and a goat leather patch at the back.

Of course, trying out any new look comes with the eternal question: How do I style these things?

Well, one of the best things about raw selvedge denim is that it wears well with pretty much everything. With that in mind, don’t overthink it. But if you do grab yourself a pair of elite-tier jeans and feel like upgrading the supporting cast around it, we have some recommendations for you. For instance, a pair of sturdy leather shoes—whether some Tyroleans, a work boot, or the like—has a multiplying effect beneath some rope-dyed indigo. The same goes for a vintage-inspired, well-proportioned t-shirt or hardy flannel. Of course, as is the case with the jeans above, not all of these items are created equal. The below eight, however, have the GQ seal of approval.

#6659. Slow Horses Season 7: Everything We Know So Far

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

After delivering a cliffhanger ending in season 6, fans of Slow Horses are wondering how the story could continue once season 7 rolls around. The fans are in luck—the MI5 agents of Slough House are clocking back in for another season, and the franchise doesn’t seem to be headed for an end anytime soon.

“I know that Gary [Oldman] has expressed a desire to play Lamb forever and that Mick [Herron] is still writing the books, so I hope it will go for as long as people want it,” the show’s executive producer, Will Smith, said in an October 2024 interview with TV Insider.

Here’s everything we know so far about Slow Horses season 7.

Yes! In July 2025, Deadline confirmed that Slow Horses would come back for a seventh season. The streaming platform greenlit the show’s seventh season before the fifth season of the show aired.

Gary Oldman, Jack Lowden, Kristin Scott Thomas, Jonathan Pryce, Hugo Weaving, Saskia Reeves, Rosalind Eleazar, Christopher Chung, Aimee-Ffion Edwards, Joanna Scanlan, Tom Brooke, Lucian Msamati, and Olivia Cooke are confirmed to return for season 7 of Slow Horses.

On October 19, Apple TV announced that Varada Sethu (Andor, Doctor Who), Ethan Moorhouse (The Moment, Ludwig), Tuppence Middleton (Downton Abbey: A New Era), Merab Ninidze (Homeland), Joshua McGuire (Anatomy of a Scandal), and James Callis (Bridget Jones’s Diary)—who is returning—will join the season 7 cast.

According to an official press release, the season “is adapted from the Bad Actors novel in the Mick Herron Slough House book series, and sees Lamb and his Slow Horses on the hunt to find and neutralize a mole at the heart of the British Government before they can bring down the state.”

The official synopsis for the book reads:

Season 7 of Slow Horses has no premiere date yet. Season 6 arrived on Apple TV in September 2026, while season 5 aired in September 2025. Season 7 could arrive sometime in fall 2027, if it follows the same timeline as the previous seasons. We’ll have to wait until Apple makes an official announcement.

Thankfully, no. Slow Horses was already renewed for season 8 in September 2026, and then Apple TV confirmed seasons 9 and 10 in November 2026. Expect a lot more from Slough House in the future.

#6657. The 12 Best-Dressed Stars at the GQ Men of the Year 2026 Party

The GQ Men of the Year 2026 party is a wrap, and what a time it was. Where else but on menswear’s biggest night could you see Stavvy rocking a chartreuse suit, get some potential dirt about the next James Bond straight from the source, and witness Matt Damon learning that “body count” has two meanings? Now that’s Hollywood, baby!

As per usual, the evening really started cooking on the step-and-repeat, where the celebs took the “modern red carpet” dress code to heart. We’re talking swaggy suiting, fantastic gowns, and yes, even a very good pair of khakis. Scroll on to see our favorite looks of the night.

Now this is how you wear a suit. The Emmy-winning star of The Bear rolled up in an impeccably tailored pinstriped look by London-based designer Conner Ives, which was punctuated by a bright green shirt, a forehead curl, and a deep burgundy tie that matched the MOTY backdrop. As GQ’s former fashion critic Rachel Tashjian put it on Instagram: “She always looks cool, but this is the coolest she’s ever looked.”

For Garfield, no look is complete without his flowing mane of hair. It doesn’t hurt to have a crisply tailored Edward Sexton suit and an all-time classic watch from Breguet on his wrist.

Andrew Garfield in Edward Sexton. Watch by Breguet.

In Mowalowa sparkles and a Donna Summer-esque ’do, Tinashe looked every bit like the Popstar she is.

The Tony star sexed up the classic shawl lapel-jacket with a high-voltage shade of green. This is what the GQ Men of the Year party is all about: pulling off a fashion risk with A-lister-level confidence.

Stavros Halkias in Alan David, Cego, and Bottega Veneta.

The writer-director duo behind this year’s hit international film, La Bola Negra, brought their own flowers last night. In addition to rocking coordinating roses, Los Javis—made up of two Javiers, Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo—put a sexy spin on the classic red-carpet suit by way of leather mesh and exposed undies (courtesy of Haider Ackermann’s Tom Ford) and perfectly tousled curls (subjects’ own).

Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo in Tom Ford.

Naturally, as GQ’s 2026 Designer of the Year, it makes sense that Rider (wearing his own Celine clothes) would be one of the best dressed of the night. Have you ever seen an undershirt peek out of a sweater with such unpracticed rakishness? Or a pair of khakis look so at home on a red carpet? Take notes.

Two episodes into the return of HBO’s Gilded Age, Louisa Jacobson cruised off a successful season premiere in a sultry McQueen moto jacket. She’s been on a style streak over the past year, with several covetable jackets and menswear-inspired outfits in her repertoire—and this leathery number is keeping that streak strong.

Louisa Jacobson in Alexander McQueen. Jewelry by Azlee.

The Off Campus breakout has spent plenty of time on red carpets this year, but a wonky striped suit by Vivienne Westwood—featuring some truly humongous lapels—is a major fashion leap forward.

Belmont Cameli in Vivienne Westwood. Watch by Audemars Piguet.

A fringed glove? A pom-pom heel? A knockout of an outfit, all courtesy of Sarah Burton’s Givenchy.

What’s better than one head full of wicked micro-whisps? Two heads full of wicked micro-whisps, as seen on GQ Breakouts Shanny Wise and Jackson Walker Lewis, of the NYC DJ duo Fcukers. They each wore all-black designer duds, punctuating their looks with cut-outs and patches of leather.

Shanny Wise in Jordan Lea Allen and Haider Ackermann. Jackson Walker Lewis in Dior and Balenciaga.

#6656. The Hot List: 20 Must-Have Pieces, According to Instagram’s Favorite Fashion Sourcer

Welcome to the Hot List, a monthly column from fashion sourcer extraordinaire Gab Waller. As a professional personal shopper to some of the best-dressed girls—she gets about 100 requests a day to track down hard-to-find wares!—Waller spends her days sourcing the most in-demand fashion and accessories. Each month, and exclusively for Vogue, she’ll deliver a cheat sheet of all the pieces she recommends you scoop up before it’s too late and the most dreaded three words in online shopping appear: “out of stock.” You can shop her personal favorites on FOUND By Gab. “This is a world in which I live and breathe,” Waller says. “I get to be a fashion detective day in and day out, and I have eyes and ears all over the globe.” Let the fashion snooping begin!

November, already!? I’m sure I’m not alone in wondering how we’re possibly already in November. This year has flown by! With Thanksgiving right around the corner, I’m starting to feel the holiday energy and can’t wait for all the festivities over the next two months to close out 2026. As parties fill up calendars, so do my DMs with requests for what to wear to each. I wanted to focus this month’s column on just that. Think velvet, sequins, extra fun colors, embellishments of all kinds, and more. Let the celebrations—and the holiday dressing—begin!

We all collectively need a go-to LBD for the holidays, and this newest style from Khaite ticks all the right boxes. I LOVE that they described it as having a doll-like silhouette. I’ll take it!

Coming in at number one are the party slipper heels from The Row that dominated my DMs. One request came through, followed by a few more, I then posted them on our stories, and as it goes, an instant hit! Now is the time to jump on these.

A snakeskin leather coat!? Say no more! One size is available now, run (or I might need to snap it up for myself!).

Including the most elegantly chic gown that will have you immediately sorted for the holidays. We may very well be matching if you choose to secure this. I love this silhouette, truly chef’s kiss!

Carolina Herrera has made its way into the Hot List, and for very good reason! If there is one must-have piece for this fall holiday season ahead, let it be a velvet jacket. The styling options are endless.

An INSTANT hit from Tory Burch. Produced last season in green, which has been highly coveted since its release, your favorite embellished bag is back this season in a new blue and black. This is one of my bestselling handbag styles this week.

The Christian Louboutin heels that speak for themselves. Already showing low stock across all sizes, I’m calling it now: these will be your go-to for any and all upcoming evening events.

If pony hair is your preferred option, look no further than this (selling fast) style from Toteme. It won’t be around for long.

Speaking of both Australian brands and pants, this new leather style from Christopher Esber has been an instant hit! Already sold out in multiple sizes, run to grab your pair now.

Ending with the return of the Idaho. No stranger to the Hot List, it has been restocked, but I can’t guarantee for how long. If you have been waiting for the perfect moment to secure this style, now is the time. It is a best seller for a reason, and for what it’s worth, the beige is my favorite!

Another Miu Miu new season style that I am predicting will sell out. The sweetest holiday dress. A couple of sizes are left, but certainly not for long.

I couldn’t resist including them in this column for the holidays. Their all new golden hour letters (available in all letters of your choosing), are the perfect holiday gift.

The quickest add to cart moment I’ve had this week! This oozes every ounce of festiveness, I love that it evokes the glamour of the roaring twenties. I anticipate a sold out style.

Certainly no stranger to this design, but this is the first time (in years!) that requests have come through for this style. I’m thrilled by this, and hope to see this only increase in time. #6655. GQ’s 2026 Men of the Year Party Brought Everyone Out

There’s no party quite like a GQ party. Who else could bring together Andrew Garfield, Robby Hoffman, Future, and Angel Reese under one roof? But that’s exactly what we did on Thursday night at Los Angeles’s famed Chateau Marmont for our 31st Men of the Year party, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label.

Following a dinner honoring our trio of cover stars—Matt Damon, Chris Rock, and Garfield—the real fun began when all three of them, along with nearly every other celebrity in town, descended on the Chateau’s garden to mix it up to the sounds of DJ Yung Tada (plus a late-night set from GQ Breakouts electro-pop duo Fcukers).

I caught Damon at the entrance to the party looking to continue our conversation from his cover story, but our reunion was cut short when Inde Navarette pulled up to say hi and exchange contacts. If the 25-year-old Obsession newcomer was starstruck by the 56-year-old Hollywood hero, the feeling seemed mutual.

Future and Travis Scott rolled up nearly at the same time; Travis, who performed the end-credits track for The Odyssey, told me he was ready to hit the Oscars campaign trail.

In every corner was a cluster of stars from different Hollywood galaxies. Abbott Elementary’s Tyler James Williams and Chris Perfetti made the rounds together, looking nothing like the harried teachers they play on TV. GQ Breakout Owen Thiele and his longtime friend Cazzie David (who gave Owen his first acting gig on her web series years ago) ignored our red carpet instructions to bless us with photogenic poses they’d pre-planned long in advance. When I asked broadcaster Taylor Rooks for an on-the-fly NBA Cup prediction, she gushed about the Celtics and the Lakers. And there was something fun about seeing Anderson .Paak and Diplo chop it up, too.

The friendly embrace shared by Austin Abrams and Skyler Gisondo, noted Good Dudes, is the unscripted team-up the internet goes nuts for. The Resident Evil and Primetime actors later shared that they’d just been on the phone together while getting ready for the party, neither realizing they’d be seeing each other shortly. When I brought up James Gunn and his recent departure from DC Studios, Gisondo called it a “bummer”—he just wrapped the “Jimmy Olsen vs. Gorilla Grodd” series, he said, and hopes that it’ll still come out (and that Gunn continues to write and direct even if he’s not in executive mode anymore).

In other unlikely but endearing encounters: Ayo Edebiri and Thiele excitedly nabbed IShowSpeed for a photo, and Lamorne Morris stopped Anthony Ippolito to give him props for I Play Rocky, counseling him to take it all in. Ippolito told me he’s headed off to Europe soon to continue promoting the film; a certified foodie, he was hunting for Paris recs (I had to put him on to HolyBelly, for the pancakes). I also caught GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, whose eyes lit up when I mentioned his woefully underrated Jake Gyllenhaal thriller Enemy.

Midway through the night I spotted Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro, who were considering an Irish exit. Garfield’s forthcoming Artificial (out December 25) is the movie on everybody’s lips, but he told me he’s looking forward to spending the holidays in New York and taking a brief break before what will probably be a busy campaign season for the Man of the Year.

No one captured the evening as succinctly as Robby Hoffman, who described her upcoming TV show as “Curb [Your Enthusiasm] for poor people.” When the conversation turned back to GQ, Hoffman rued the decline of magazine paper quality. But this latest issue got her seal of approval: appropriately glossy, well-considered, and elite to the touch. Though she might have just been describing the party’s guest list.

But even if you didn’t make the cut, you can see how GQ’s Men of the Year 2026 party looked from the inside. ✦

#6654. Loaded Mashed Potatoes

Mashed potatoes are a classic side dish that can make almost any meal better. They’re creamy, fluffy, and nearly perfect…nearly. When thinking of how to improve on a dish already so close to perfection, I decided to go back to the basics. What’s the best kind of potato? A loaded baked potato. With this in mind, I combined the two superstar spuds into one glorious dish. In it, light, airy mashed potatoes are topped with all of the classic baked potato fillings—cheddar cheese, chives, bacon, and sour cream—for a dish that truly embodies the best of both worlds.

The beauty of these potatoes is that they can go with any number of dinners. Serve them alongside your favorite protein—chicken, steak, pork chops, the world is your oyster—or alongside a few lighter sides like any of our green salads, caramelized Brussels sprouts, or roasted green beans.

Any leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for 3 to 4 days. If you haven’t already added the toppings, store them separately. Whatever you do, don’t let leftovers go to waste. We’ve got plenty of leftover mashed potato recipes to make sure you get the most out of the special spuds.

#6653. 37 Family Dinner Ideas You’ll Make on Repeat

The good news about “family-friendly” dinners? They can be whatever you want them to be. Loaded sweet potato wedges eaten straight from the sheet pan? Absolutely. A dose of nostalgia by way of movie-night sloppy Joes, updated with a fiery kick of gochujang? No question about it. These are dinners for cautious eaters and adventurous ones alike—some familiar, some a little unexpected, and all worth bringing to the table.

Whether tonight calls for a cozy soup (that you can set and forget in your Instant Pot) or easy fish tacos (we have a hunch they’ll become part of your regular weeknight dinner rotation), we’ve got plenty of ideas to keep dinner interesting all year long.

Set tortillas, flaky cod or halibut, spicy lime sauce, and toppings out family-style and let everyone assemble their own piled-high tacos. It’s a simple weeknight family dinner that doubles as a choose-your-own-adventure activity.

Packed with ground chicken, white beans, and canned green chiles, this fast-cooking stew only gets better over time, so make a big batch. We promise, you won’t mind eating it two days in a row.

High-protein cottage cheese replaces often-pricier ricotta in this thrifty-ish spin on a familiar family favorite. More shocking: mozzarella is out too, in favor of tangy super-melter Fontina.

If your family loves pepperoni pizza, they’ll love this baked pasta, which hits all the saucy, spicy, cheesy notes with no takeout required. Roasting the sauce on a sheet pan concentrates its flavor before everything gets a blanket of cheese.

All the appeal of a spicy salmon roll, reassembled as a family-friendly bowl. Pickled cucumber and spicy mayo accompany crackly, broiled salmon cubes for a dinner that’s as fun to eat as it is easy to customize.

Smoky-sweet Korean gochujang lends a hum of heat to this riff on a childhood favorite. Soft buns and a stack of napkins do the rest.

Think chicken pot pie, but in cozy soup form. Complete with crackly, buttery shards of puff pastry you can tear and share, this family meal practically demands a crowd around the table.

This shareable skillet is packed with the flavors of a family-favorite appetizer, with roasted poblanos, red onions, and jalapeños smothered in cheesy sauce.

Store-bought pizza dough makes this family-friendly dinner a snap, even on busy weeknights. This California Pizza Kitchen-inspired recipe is smoky-sweet thanks to barbecue sauce, Gouda cheese, and frizzled mushrooms.

Store-bought zhug, a Yemeni-spiced cilantro sauce, and your broiler are the shortcuts to juicy, charred, baked chicken without a grill. It’s an easy, low-fuss dinner that delivers big flavor.

Somewhere between nachos and loaded potatoes, roasted sweet potatoes get topped with spiced ground beef and briny kimchi for a main dish that’s complete enough to enjoy straight off the sheet pan.

Genuinely juicy, supremely crispy, flavored like falafel, and browned in a skillet for ultimate ease. Serve them with your favorite burger toppings for an easy family dinner.

Sometimes you just want to cook an old faithful—the kind of dinner you know the whole family will love. That’s when you reach for this rich, cheesy, ever-reliable baked ziti.

These vibrant (and vegetarian) kale-and-black-bean-stuffed peppers are a repeat-worthy, one-dish dinner full of hearty flavor. Stirring a dollop of sour cream into the tomato sauce gives it rich texture.

Everyone loves a customizable dinner, and this shawarma-spiced chicken is made for it. Set out warm pitas and all your favorite fixings, like sliced tomatoes and cucumber spears, and let everyone build their perfect plate.

Shrimp cooked in garlicky, lemony butter is bound to be delicious. Serve it with crusty bread or toss it with pasta for a cozy weeknight meal the whole family will love.

Golden-edged tofu meets a bold, spicy satay-inspired peanut sauce in this quick, satisfying dish. Pile it over rice or serve with naan for scooping.

Canned pumpkin is good for way more than sweets. Here, lemon, Parmesan, and chile flakes turn it into a creamy, savory sauce that comes together while the pasta boils.

Spinach-packed dal is a lifesaver on nights when you’re strapped for time but craving something deeply comforting. Serve it with rice or flatbread for a quick vegetarian meal.

Tender soy-glazed chicken meatballs and crisp sesame green beans make a balanced family dinner that needs little else than a pot of rice.

Transform two favorite store-bought ingredients—cheese ravioli and crispy fried onions—into a rich and luscious skillet dinner with a crispy, savory top.

This sunny, dressed-for-summer family dinner relies on a pantry-friendly chicken marinade. All you need: sugar, vinegar, salt, and a few spices. Add couscous and dinner is done.

Make these succulent pork chops when it’s 6:26 p.m. on a Monday and you haven’t figured out what’s for dinner. The sweet-and-savory sauce makes this quick weeknight meal feel planned ahead.

Canned chickpeas and frozen broccoli keep this one-skillet dinner fast and thrifty, while cream cheese delivers on the faux pasta Alfredo front.

Leftover rice meets plenty of fresh ginger, soy sauce, and eggs in this satisfying 20-minute dinner. The key is starting with cold, cooked rice, which crisps up beautifully in a hot skillet.

Cherry tomatoes burst around a block of feta in the oven, forming a tangy, creamy pasta sauce. Calabrian chile paste brings a welcome kick that cuts through the richness.

This hearty catch-all skillet dinner tastes just as good in egg burritos the next morning, or make and freeze it up to three months ahead.

Upgrade grilled salmon with a punchy, vibrant dill chimichurri. It’s quick, fresh, and feels fancy enough to make you feel like you have your life together.

Much faster to make than risotto, this lemony, bright orzotto gets its herby savoriness from a pantry savior: store-bought jarred pesto.

Your favorite party dip, now in pasta form. Frozen spinach and jarred artichokes keep things convenient, while plenty of bubbling cheese makes this skillet dinner every bit as comforting as the original.

So tired you’re considering takeout? Try this simple, speedy stir-fry instead—it comes together in 25 minutes but tastes restaurant-quality.

Store-bought gnocchi bakes up crispy on the outside and pillowy on the inside, the perfect complement to browned spicy sausage and a sprinkle of finely grated Parmesan.

Give mac and cheese the hot wing treatment, because sometimes one comfort food just isn’t enough. It’s creamy, tangy, and just spicy enough to keep you coming back for another forkful.

Let your Instant Pot handle this warm, spicy, protein-packed, family-friendly dinner idea. Top it with a dollop of sour cream, a sprinkle of pickled onions, and whatever else floats your fancy.

Chicken and cabbage may sound pretty basic, but this stir-fry is anything but. Sambal oelek and fish sauce give it plenty of spicy, salty flavor, making it a nutritious family dinner that packs a punch.

Crisp bibb lettuce leaves make the perfect cups for this spicy larb-inspired chicken, which you can dress up with fresh herbs and fried shallots. It’s a fun, hands-on family dinner that gets everyone involved.

This is the kind of salad that can hold its own as a family dinner, packed with roasted sweet potato and tofu, crisp red apple, and a bright, herby green goddess dressing.

#6652. Read Dodie Kazanjian’s In-Depth 1994 Richard Avedon Profile for Vogue

“Avedon’s Eye,” by Dodie Kazanjian, was originally published in the February 1994 issue of Vogue.

For more of the best from Vogue’s archive, sign up for our Nostalgia newsletter here.

Richard Avedon made four trips to Stockholm a few years ago to see Ingmar Bergman’s production of Long Day’s Journey into Night, in Swedish. He saw it seven times. “There’s no movie I could see seven times, but when a great living performance captures me, I could go every night, forever . . . . At the Royal Dramatic Theater in Stockholm, when you go upstairs for coffee during intermission, there’s a place on the ceiling where they have the masks of comedy and tragedy—and they’re both tragedy! Because you’re in Sweden. So it’s the perfect place for me, obviously.”

There’s some irony here but also a valid point. Theater is the guiding metaphor in Richard Avedon’s life, as well as his work. An element of drama gets into everything he does, and the last few months have certainly brought him center stage. The most famous American photographer of our time has been up to his ears in publicity (and controversy) over his recently published book of photographs—which he calls An Autobiography—and over the major retrospective of his work that opens on March 24 at the Whitney Museum. Attention is being paid: 30 pages in Newsweek on the man and his work; appearances on Prime-Time Live, the Today show, and Charlie Rose; a black-tie gala at the New York Public Library for 300 people, thrown by husband-and-wife team Harold Evans, head of Random House (which published An Autobiography), and Tina Brown, The New Yorker’s editor, who a year ago made Avedon the magazine’s first and only staff photographer. At the age of 70, Avedon has shifted his half-century career into overdrive, but somehow he still manages to find time to make dinner arrangements with this reporter for a gourmet meal that he cooks himself.

In a manner of speaking, that is. “You call this cooking?” Dick scoffs, in his unmistakable rasp—New York accented but with other ingredients, mostly untraceable. “I’m an executive cook,” he says. Verlie Fisher, his longtime housekeeper, made the herbed chicken that afternoon and left foolproof instructions for heating it up. We are in the kitchen and dining area of his loft, a vast and monumentally cluttered space on the second floor of an Upper East Side town house that was once a commercial laundry. The legendary Avedon studio is downstairs, the main part of it anyway; additional workspaces for his team of fifteen associates have taken root on the two floors above his living quarters. Your first impression here is that there’s too much of everything. There are seventeen different-size lighted candles on the long dining table, and bowls of blueberries and blackberries and nuts and cheeses, and photographs both framed and unframed, and pots of narcissus and orchids, and an out-of-control bamboo tree that brushes the ceiling, and a bright red leather boxing glove that’s just arrived from Paris. (“Since this was a rough week for me, a French friend sent it over.”)

Avedon is in constant motion, checking the oven, darting here and there, running his fingers through his long silver-white hair, reaching under his glasses to rub his eyes. A lithe, compact bundle of nervous energy, he is wearing blue jeans, loafers without socks, and a blue shirt with ASTAIRE LIVES printed on the pocket; he had it put there because this was the shirt he was wearing when he heard that Fred Astaire, his childhood idol, had just died. With Avedon, conversation doesn’t just flow—it runs and jumps and turns on a dime and sometimes goes in two or more directions at once. In the fifteen minutes before dinner is ready, he covers the origins of his three favorite chicken recipes (Janet Cam’s Buddhist Chicken, Marcella Hazan’s Chicken with Three Lemons, and Verlie’s own Herbed Chicken); Chekhov’s short stories— “Did you know that he wrote 300? I’ve ordered the whole thirteen-volume set”; his son John’s work as a foreign relations adviser to and biographer of the Dalai Lama of Tibet; the young boxer in Phoenix, whom he photographed for The New Yorker yesterday; the three negative reviews of An Autobiography in The New York Times, which should have killed sales of the $100 book but didn’t; and the critical knives that are being whetted for his Whitney show, which was viciously attacked by Hilton Kramer in The New York Observer two years in advance of its opening. (“This is the ultimate capitulation to celebrity, money and fashion at the expense of art.”) “Reviews no longer victimize me,” Avedon says. “Or define me, or elate me, or stop me from working.”

In The New York Times Book Review, Maud Lavin wrote, “Mr. Avedon’s close, hard stare, his emptied backgrounds and his graphically spectacular compositions do not tell us any more about the social context of napalm victims than they do about fashion models. These techniques do not unmask the ambiguities of people’s lives. What they demonstrate is the extraordinary high degree of control Mr. Avedon exerts in all his confrontations with his subjects.” In the daily Times, Margo Jefferson said of the portraits in Avedon’s book, “By the end, I was rooting for anyone who managed to escape with a shred of self-determination intact.” Andy Grundberg’s more recent notice in the Book Review said that An Autobiography showed Avedon “at his most characteristic: controlling of his subjects and manipulative of his audience, driven to redeem himself from the taint of commerce, obsessed with the judgments of a disembodied posterity.”

Why does Avedon get attacked so savagely? His tremendous success as a fashion photographer is one obvious reason: How dare he presume to be an artist as well? Avedon has fought this dichotomy all his professional life, insisting that there is no difference between his fashion work, his reportage, and the body of portraiture that is his principal claim to recognition as an artist. “I think art history will see him as one of the great portraitists of the twentieth century,” says David Ross, the Whitney’s director, who has come in for a lot of abuse himself over his decision to present an Avedon retrospective. “He’s spent so much of his life in analysis, and in the quest of understanding who he is—this tortured, self-driven Jewish man who is trying to understand himself by looking at other people and their lives, and looking at the way things work, and trying to see into that borderline area between madness and beauty and power and powerlessness. He’s looked hard, as all great artists do.”

Ross insists that working with Avedon on the Whitney retrospective did not involve pitched battles over who was in control. “When we started working on this show, I said to Dick, ‘This is the show that needs to be done for you, not by you; you need to have that happen, as every artist does.’ On the design level, Dick was as directorial as ever. You would have to be a complete fool not to make use of Dick and Mary Shanahan, an amazing designer who works with him. But on a curatorial level, he really let Jane Livingston choose the show. The primary selection of pictures, the primary story that’s being told in the show and in the catalog, is Jane’s.”

The oven timer announces that the chicken is ready. He carves it deftly, serves it with his special house salad—tiny mâche lettuce leaves and shaved Parmesan. The bread is folded into the napkins to keep it fresh. The wine is a 1987 Margaux. The plates are oversize Italian faience from Siena, boldly colorful against the deep blue tablecloth. “You mustn’t think that I care about candle colors and tablecloths and stuff like that,” he says. He does care, nevertheless. It’s all part of the Avedon performance, a never-ending engagement with the visual world in all its forms.

Is it unfair to say that Avedon’s portraits are manipulative, overly controlled, and “trapped in narcissism,” as Maud Lavin charged in The New York Times? This criticism is often heard, and to some extent it may be justified. But then, all great portraits are in a sense self-portraits, and all artists exercise manipulation and control. When Avedon takes a portrait, it is the record of an intense, indelibly personal encounter between the photographer and the subject, whether the subject happens to be a fashion model or a drifter, an actor or a napalm victim, ex-president Dwight David Eisenhower or Jacob Israel Avedon, the photographer’s 87-year-old father, dying of cancer. And if there is sometimes more of Richard Avedon than of the subject in this encounter, well, that’s all in the nature of the performance that Avedon demands in his life and work. But what if the subject won’t perform? Doesn’t this happen in his current avatar as The New Yorker’s staff photographer? “Oh, yes,” he says. “Of course. I’m about as interested in David Dinkins and Rudy Giuliani . . . but that’s part of the job. I’m quite willing to do photographs that are not pure expressions of myself, like the one of Steve Martin on the wall here. He was enormously generous in the sitting, but there’s no such thing as cutting through to Steve Martin. Steve Martin uses his comic genius like a wall. There’s no penetrating it, and I respect that.” Later, he shows me the note Steve Martin sent him after the sitting: "Dear Richard, Yours was the first photo shoot I ever enjoyed . . . . I hope we can become very close friends forsaking all others and have lunches and dinners together six days a week.”

David Ross told me a story about watching Avedon at work on his photographic series called In the American West. “One of the great emblematic West pictures is of a guy with his shirt half over his shoulders. He has a kind of S-shaped body. I remember seeing that guy on the midway of a state fair in southern Colorado. He was the kind of guy I would have crossed the street to avoid. He was tough, and angry, and on the line of being psychotic, and all my good Jewish radar tells me stay away, no eye contact, keep moving. But Dick goes right up and starts talking to him, and within five minutes he is pouring his energy out for Dick in front of a white drop cloth tacked up on a side of a shed. It was astounding to see how he communicates and puts people at ease and allows them to come through.”

Dick is slightly displeased with himself over the chicken. “A little dry, don’t you think? It’s so nice when it’s really juicy. I think we didn’t need that last fifteen minutes.” He has another helping anyway. And he orders me to strip my wishbone clean so he can hang it on the lip of a special pitcher that holds ten or twelve others. “I still have wishes,” he says. “Being 70 doesn’t preclude that.” Dinner consists of one main course plus dessert, simple but extravagant. Another time, you might have a baked potato smothered in beluga caviar, or the special borscht that he carried home in a cardboard container one night from a Russian restaurant in Brighton Beach—he enriches it with piroshki. If he’s serving pasta, it will be Cipriani’s, or else mushroom pasta by his friend China Machado, who was once one of his models and now has a store in Water Mill. Long Island. He jumps up and brings over a box of the Cipriani pasta from the open larder shelves on which are stacked sixteen others. “Just try one of these,” he says of the Cipriani masterpiece. “It takes about a minute and a half to cook. It’s all egg.”

A few days earlier, he had told me that I didn’t have an “Avedon face.” I ask him what he means by an Avedon face. “It’s very varied,” he says. “One of the great Avedon faces is Michelangelo Antonioni’s. There are artists just as complicated as Antonioni, but their complexity isn’t available to my camera. Fellini’s was not an Avedon face. Roy Lichtenstein’s is. I can’t explain it exactly. It’s not about being ravaged or flawed. It’s about contradictions, dialogue, arguments. The soul’s confusion on the face.”

Even in his fashion work he captured that confusion, as Penelope Tree attested in a letter to Avedon about her portrait in An Autobiography. “Of course I identified with being caged, isolated, and utterly bewildered, but I thought I was doing a better job of hiding it! Trust you to see right through. I guess you always did.”

The encounter between Avedon and subject is what makes the portrait, and that usually has a lot to do with what Avedon is feeling at the moment he takes the photograph. Does this make him a monster egoist, as some of his critics maintain? Or is he simply doing what Titian, Velázquez, Francis Bacon, or any great artist does? “Of course, of course,” he says. “Art isn’t art because someone uses a paintbrush. Photography is either good or bad, and when it’s good it’s like any art that’s good. It becomes Art.

“What the subject brings to the camera and what I do with that is what makes the photograph. In photographing my father,” he says, referring to the famous series of his father dying, “I was looking at him. and he was looking at me. The last thing he saw as he was dying was his son. It’s clear to me that he became, in that moment, in that image, what he saw. And what he saw was me.”

Avedon had his own portrait taken for this article. He chose the photographer: his great contemporary and rival, Irving Penn. On the day of the sitting. Avedon had the flu and such severe stomach pains that he called his doctor, from Penn’s studio, for a prescription. “Will I be loopy if I take it?” he asked. “I have an interview with the London Times right after this, and then I’m flying to Hyannis Port to photograph Ethel Kennedy.” “No loopier than usual” was the doctor’s reply. Avedon had brought along a legendary coat from the fifties to be photographed in, a heavy old shearling that he had won in a bet with the model Suzy Parker; it had once warmed Marilyn Monroe, and Isabelle Adjani had worn it in an Avedon photograph. Penn took some shots of him in the coat, but the image that won out shows him in an open-collared work shirt, looking haunted and strangely romantic. “He has a drama that we got that I don’t associate with him,” Penn said afterward. “Like something out of the French Revolution.”

Although Avedon had been photographed twice before by Penn, he tells me that this was the first time he had felt “ready” for the experience. “It’s a wonderful picture,” he says, “the only real portrait of me by Penn. Maybe by anybody. He’s caught something. The real strength of any portrait is to go beneath the surface and into the contradictions within the life. And he’s done that so completely in this portrait. It’s about a kind of crumbling part of me that’s a cross between arrogance and suspicion. Penn’s portrait has nothing to do with looking good, and in this case, it has very little to do with composition. It has a rawness—I mean, it’s more of an Avedon than a Penn. Ha! And yet it could never have been taken by anyone but Penn.”

What is the difference between an Avedon portrait and a Penn portrait?

“I think Penn’s great strength lies in his power of composition and in the very still moment that reveals. From the beginning, I’ve felt that any composition that is visible in my photographs takes you away from the direct confrontation that I look for. If anyone said of a picture of mine. ‘Look at the composition in that,’ I’d be embarrassed. I’d know that I failed.

“Rivalry is a funny word to use about Penn and me. It doesn’t cover or even hint at the relationship. In the years when I was at Harper’s Bazaar [ 1945 to 1965] and he was at Vogue, and we were both covering the same celebrities, I watched every move he made, and I think in some way it helped define me. I was always excited by Penn, in awe of Penn, and wanted to top him or equal him, or be the opposite of him. I think of him as a classicist and of me as an eclectic. I was fired by him. inspired by him. pushed by his standards, his rigor, his excellence.”

I ask him which other photographers he has admired. “Certainly Diane Arbus, Julia Margaret Cameron in the old days. But Cartier-Bresson rules. Walker Evans is a miniaturist compared to him. There are wonderful photographers—Robert Frank, for example—who have mastered small areas of the territory Cartier-Bresson laid out. The world of photojournalism is littered with Bresson babies. He is the photographic Tolstoy of the twentieth century.

“Helmut Newton redefined what a fashion photograph could be. He’s the leader of the post-Avedon, post-Penn period. He released everything. He changed what a fashion model could look like and played with vulgarity in a really witty way. After Helmut Newton, you can’t do a certain kind of picture anymore.”

“It’s done all the time, and it’s boring! But when Helmut does it, the erotic focus shifts from the ankle and the smile to the inner thigh.”

It’s a little odd to hear Richard Avedor speak of the post-Avedon, post-Penn period. Bruce Weber, one of today’s top fashion photographers who photographed Avedon for this article, sees his influence as being very much alive and in the present. “Richard Avedon is like this wonderful kid you meet at school, who has more energy than anybody else,” Weber says. “He really is open, he engages you in what’s going on in his life, and he makes you then think about your own. He’s influenced a whole generation of photographers who are working now, me included, in that just simply and purely you want to take photographs and to photograph your own life at the same time. Dick’s work is not about fame. It’s really about still being a kid and not being afraid to shoe it.”

We’re heavily into dessert by this time. Dick always serves at least five—three different ice and an orange cake from Sant Ambroeus, fresh blackberries and raspberries, macaroons from Bonté, and a split of the Billecart-Salmon champagne that he discovered years ago at Chez Panisse. He promises next time to make Mike Nichols’s Peach Orgasm (six fresh peaches, two bananas, one and a half cups of sugar, two cups of sour cream, and the juice of one lemon: blend in blender, then put in ice cream maker). He has a file of recipes that he’s picked up from restaurants and friends in various parts of the world. It’s more than enough for a book, but it will have to wait until he’s finished the ten books he’s already under contract to do for Random House: several more collections of his photographs: four teaching books based on his master classes in fashion photography, reportage, portraiture, and the snapshot; and an autobiographical novel that he says he’ll be working on for the rest of his life.

There’s another kind of autobiography on the walls. Hundreds of photographs, clippings, postcards, notes, mementos, and reproductions of famous paintings are pinned to the soft beaverboard, some of them yellow with age. Shots of Fred Astaire dancing, and one of Astaire with the young Avedon during the filming of Funny Face, in which the great dancer played the part of a fashion photographer based on Richard Avedon. A more mature Avedon with Audrey Hepburn, Miss Funny Face herself. The New York Post’s front page on Liz Taylor’s eighth marriage, with eight “I Do’s” in bold type. Three Avedon press cards for the year he went to Vietnam. A news photo of an unidentified man frozen to death beneath the ice of a lake in Queens, New York. Athletes in violent action. Snapshots of Evelyn, his wife, whom he hasn’t lived with for many years (he still sees her for dinner or a movie at least once a week), and one of their son, John, and John’s wife, Maura Moynihan, the senator’s daughter, with their son, Michael. A blown-up page of The New York Times Magazine with head shots of seventeen people whom Stalin had killed. (“They were photographed and then they were killed,” Avedon says. “Look, aren’t these the most pure and perfect portraits?”) A life-size blowup of Ruby Holden, the Nevada pawnbroker whom Avedon photographed in 1980. A poster of Goya’s Contessa Chinchón, which he considers one of the great portraits in Western art—”an infantile woman in an evening gown,” he says. “A combination of fashion and portraiture. Most portraiture involves fashion. That’s what Penn does. That’s what I try to do.”

Fashion photographs, by Avedon or anyone else, are nonetheless conspicuously absent from this wall of memories and momentary enthusiasms. No Dovima with elephants, no Suzy Parker, no Twiggy, no Jean Shrimpton or Stephanie Seymour, his current favorite. Other than a few isolated examples, only one room (out of fifteen) at the Whitney retrospective will be devoted to Avedon’s fashion work, and this makes you wonder about his reiterated argument that all his work, fashion included, is a part of the same seamless web. Avedon’s ambivalent relationship with the world of high fashion, which has given him the means to pursue his ambitions as an artist, was exacerbated in 1988 when he had a falling out with Vogue’s new editor. He had photographed almost every Vogue cover since 1966 but found he disagreed with Anna Wintour about how Vogue covers should look, and she stopped using him for covers. Recently, on the occasion of this interview, he wrote Wintour a letter and signed it “Let’s bury the lipsticks. Dick.” In the meanwhile, he has not lacked for commercial outlets. Tomorrow he starts a big job for Versace—racks of dresses and underwear and tables of accessories have taken over the far end of the long room, for a weeklong shoot that will be the firm’s next major ad campaign.

The problem is he won’t be using Stephanie Seymour, who is pregnant. “I’ll never forgive her,” he says, mock-seriously. Avedon has always liked to work more or less exclusively with one model at a time. Suzy Parker, his favorite of the fifties, has vivid memories of their working relationship. “We had become so attuned to each other,” she tells me. “First of all, we shared an outrageous sense of humor. Second, we worked to music, so we were already into movement. I mean, I was never still. Before Dick, modeling was like being crucified most of the time. They’d have tissue paper stuffed up your dress, they’d have clothespins and safety pins up and down your back. They’d have strings that wouldn’t show to hold the movement of the skirt. The whole thing was absolutely ghastly. With Dick it was always movement. And I was young enough to walk out on one of the gargoyle heads of Nôtre Dame. Nobody else would do that. I was young enough to go out on high heels on one of those beams of the Eiffel Tower. I did roller-skating on cobblestones. He would set up these crazy situations.” Penelope Tree, one of his favorites in the sixties, says that “when you worked with Dick, you were so caught up in the moment, some intensely personal sort of moment. I’ve never had that experience with any other photographer before or since. It was really like having a love affair, except it wasn’t at all physical.”

The back wall, behind the Versace paraphernalia, is crowded with images of a different sort. Above low bookshelves filled with art books are framed photographs by Baron de Meyer, Atget, Brassaï, Man Ray, Cameron, and Avedon, most of them of disturbed-looking women. Also an Avedon portrait of his father that was the poster for his 1974 show at the Museum of Modern Art, and one of his horrific images of a grimacing Oscar Levant, which Avedon sometimes considers his finest portrait. The dark side of the Avedon psyche is in command here. (Avedon: “It is through the dark part of the eye that we see light.”) Nearby on the side wall is a huge blowup of four grimy coal miners, from the American West series. “I like that one less and less,” he says. “My hand is just too strong in it. Just too much of me manipulating. The craftsmanship, the composition. It’s all too apparent. It doesn’t reach below the surface.”

He laughs and makes a sweeping gesture that somehow includes the room and everything in it. “You know what I’m going to do? Empty this place out. Put everything on the walls in boxes, or the warehouse or the fire. I’ll just dump everything and start again, see who I become. Try to do it better, more deeply, and if I lose it, hope that my friends shoot me or at least stop me from becoming Steichen, photographing the apple tree outside my window with a new young wife kneeling at my feet.”

There’s a brick fireplace that Avedon never uses because pigeons have nested in the chimney. The mantel is cluttered with stuff, like every other flat surface here. An empty bottle of 1923 Lafite-Rothschild, Avedon’s birth year, stands on a boxed bottle of the same vintage, undrunk, “waiting for the right occasion.” There are also three parcels in brown wrapping paper, tied in ordinary string, unopened. He knows what one of them is—a bleached-white skeleton of a bird’s wing that washed up on the beach of Antigua years ago, during a photographic shoot with Suzy Parker; Dick and Suzy both wanted it, and it became their “bone of contention,” which travels back and forth between them. The other two boxes, he says, “I hope to open just before I die. They’re from someone who means a great deal to me. If I’m alone when I die, opening them—discovering what’s in there—will be like the right person holding my hand.”

It’s a quarter to twelve, way after his bedtime. He wakes up at five every morning, gets out of bed at six, turns the coffee on, and does last night’s dishes “for therapy.” Breakfast is coffee and fresh apple juice, squeezed by Verlie from whole apples the day before. His personal trainer comes three mornings a week at 7:30 to give him a one-hour workout. When he says good night, his voice is a little raspier, but his restless energy shows no signs of flagging.

It’s the next morning, 7:30, and Avedon is calling in great agitation. He says last night’s interview “didn’t work,” and we have to try again. This time he’ll invite his old and close friend Twyla Tharp, and he tells me I can be a fly on the wall while they wing it conversationally. OK, I say, well aware that there’s no arguing with Avedon in his control-freak mood. I go, I listen, I’m charmed, I’m well fed—lamb roast and applesauce with horseradish, homemade pumpkin pie and the usual cornucopia of desserts. His son, John, is there, and John’s nearly three-year-old son, Michael. So are the seventeen candles, which almost send the bamboo tree up in flames. It’s a warm, family sort of evening, and the conversation goes off in two dozen directions, and if it were reproduced here, we could have yet another portrait of Richard Avedon. The possibilities are endless. •

#6651. Upside-Down Cream Of Mushroom Tartlets

Upside-down tartlets went viral on social media, but they’re the party app we’re forever obsessed with. This hack uses store-bought puff pastry and transforms it into a beautiful, shareable snack filled with your sweet or savory filling of choice. Here, we’re leaning into cozy season by creating a cream of mushroom soup-inspired filling that pairs perfectly with the flaky pastry.

The mushrooms:You can find mushrooms used in two different ways here: both sliced and in a creamy, cheesy filling. The filling starts with a classic combination of minced mushrooms and shallots known as a duxelles (the very same mixture you can find at the base of a beef Wellington). To make this filling more mushroom soup-esque, we supplement it with Gùyere, heavy cream, and either sour cream or crème fraîche. The tangy dairy offsets some of the richness of the pastry while still containing enough fat to avoid curdling in the oven.

The pastry:When working with puff pastry, it’s important that you avoid prolonged exposure to heat. The dough is stacked with layers and layers of cold butter, which should melt and produce steam in the oven to create that signature flaky texture. Allowing that butter to melt while the dough sits on the counter will sacrifice that essential puff. If you notice your pastry start to warm up or stick to the counter, transfer it to a parchment-lined baking sheet, and let it cool down in the refrigerator for 10 to 15 minutes before you start working with it again.

Make ahead:The best part about this recipe is that you can make most of the components ahead of time. The mushroom filling can be made up to 3 days in advance, while the puff pastry squares can be cut and refrigerated up to a day before serving.

#6649. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6648. Bon Appétit Pick: HelloFresh Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls

Over the past few years, BA editors have tested just about every meal delivery service out there, and HelloFresh keeps standing out for its bold flavors. So we teamed up with the brand on a 12-week collaboration. The BA Picks collection features recipes hand-selected by our staff, and HelloFresh customers also get an exclusive three-month digital subscription to Bon Appétit. To choose them, we cooked many, many kits in our home kitchens and in the BA Test Kitchen, following the recipe cards exactly. We judged each one on flavor, portion size, cook time, cuisine variety, and the recipe's step-by-step clarity. This Ginger Chicken and Rice Bowl is one of those picks. Here’s what it’s like to make it at home.

As a product tester, I'm very methodical, so I was excited to help build the BA Picks collection. I got to cook a bunch of meals and decide which ones were the best—the same process I take when testing the best pizza ovens or juicers. Despite being Italian, I'm constantly drawn to Asian flavors when I cook at home on weeknights. The balance of salty, sweet, spicy, and acidic is highly addictive. It hits the spot after a long day of reviewing appliances in the Test Kitchen.

That's why the Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls caught my eye. Made with soy, Thai chili sauce, gochujang, ponzu, and Korean chili flakes, it has all the flavors I crave. It reminded me of some of my favorite BA recipes, like our Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry, a mainstay in my weeknight rotation. Can a meal kit recipe stand up to a Bon Appétit recipe that's tested over weeks of development? It was my job to find out. (Spoiler alert: It did.)

HelloFresh's Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls pair saucy ginger chicken with rice, a spicy cucumber side, and toasted peanuts on top. The recipe card rates it easy and lists a total time of 20 minutes. You can order it in two-, three-, four-, or six-serving sizes.

I have an entire container in my fridge dedicated to Asian condiments. If I were cooking this recipe from scratch, I'd have to lug the whole thing out, and the bottles would cover my counter. HelloFresh measures everything out for you, so all you have to do is open the bags and follow the step-by-step instructions.

This kit came with a "mini" cucumber that was more like a normal-size one (perfect for me, since I love cucumber salad). It also had all the seasonings, rice, toppings like peanuts, and chopped chicken breast.

The pre-chopped chicken was the underrated MVP. I rarely cook chicken at home because I hate handling it raw, plus the cleanup that comes after. (Always sanitize your cutting board and prep station after working with raw meat!) So HelloFresh came in clutch here. The only ingredients I had to pull from my own pantry were oil, salt, pepper, and a small dash of sugar.

HelloFresh instructions include photos of each step, so they're easy to follow. I started by putting a pot of rice on. Then I chopped and salted the cucumbers so they could season while I cooked the chicken. After a quick sauté in a pan, I tossed the chicken in the sauce, and it was ready. Once I drained the cucumbers, all I had to do was add the chili flakes, gochujang, sesame oil, ponzu, and sugar. From start to finish, the whole process took me all of 20 minutes. That was great, because the smells coming from each component were making my mouth water.

This dish exceeded my expectations for a meal kit. The cucumbers got a ton of umami from the fermented gochujang dressing, and the chicken was saucy, with a punch of ponzu. The ginger sauce has it all: a sweet, mild ginger flavor, a trace of salty soy, and a hint of heat. Thai chili sauce and ponzu turn it into a sticky glaze for the chicken. The cucumbers add a cooling side and a pop of color, and the peanuts on top are the finishing touch. These are flavors I'd never expect in a delivery box, and I'm super impressed.

Anyone looking to explore Asian ingredients would learn a lot from this dish. It uses gochujang, ponzu, Thai chili sauce, and Korean chili flakes. I'd never cooked with Korean chili flakes (also known as gochugaru), so I was excited to taste it. If you want a quick dinner, this recipe comes together in just 20 minutes. It's a flavorful dish without project-level effort.

The Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls hit the salty, sweet, spicy, and acidic balance I crave after a long day. The pre-chopped chicken and photo-guided steps make it easy, and there's no counter full of condiments to put away afterward. Find it in the BA Picks collection on HelloFresh, along with an exclusive three-month digital subscription to Bon Appétit.

#6646. Wendy's Is Making Major Changes To Its Menu—Including A Creamier Frosty

Wendy's is giving its classics an upgrade.

Wendy's is betting that better bacon and a creamier Frosty could help its sales slump. After reporting another decline in U.S. sales, the fast food chain is testing changes to several of its best-known menu items. This refresh will appear on the menu at some point in 2027, according to Fox News.

The most interesting update might be the Frosty, which Wendy's is working to make richer and creamier. The chain hasn't revealed the exact recipe changes, but given how recognizable the dessert has become, I'm curious how much the new version will differ. Whether or not it wins over fans who already know and love the original consistency is also up in the air.

Then there's the bacon. Wendy's is testing thicker, crispier bacon that could give sandwiches like the Baconator a more substantial bite. Personally, I think this is a pretty smart move. There's nothing more disappointing than ordering a bacon cheeseburger and barely noticing the bacon.

The chain is also experimenting with whole-leaf lettuce on sandwiches and upgraded salads, all part of an effort to improve the quality of its existing menu rather than relying entirely on new products.

These changes aren’t coming out of nowhere. Wendy's reported a 5.7% decline in U.S. same-restaurant sales during the third quarter of 2026, marking another difficult period for the chain. In response, CEO Bob Wright is introducing a multi-year turnaround strategy called “Dave's Way,” named after Wendy's founder Dave Thomas.

The strategy focuses on improving the menu, marketing, restaurant operations, and digital ordering experience while giving customers better value for their money. But depending on your nearest location, it might come at a cost: breakfast.

Wendy's is allowing franchise operators to decide whether offering breakfast makes financial sense for their individual restaurants. That means some locations could stop serving breakfast altogether, although the company isn't eliminating the morning menu nationwide.

Wendy's also plans to simplify its offerings by removing lower-selling items that make restaurant kitchens more complicated to operate. However, the chain hasn't provided a complete list of products that could disappear.

The chain is still testing upgraded ingredients, so we won’t know the extent of the menu refresh or when it’ll roll out until some point in 2027. But if you’re anything like me, you’ll be waiting with bated breath to see how Wendy’s changes one of the most iconic fast food desserts.

#6645. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.
